name: Chinese (Mandarin)
summary: Mandarin is a clear isolating language: no word ever changes its form, and grammar is carried by a fixed word order (subject – time – place – verb – object, every modifier before its head) and by small separate words — measure words between numbers and nouns, aspect particles (了, 过, 着) with no tenses, sentence-final particles for mood, coverbs before the verb and place words after the noun with no cases. Every syllable has a lexical tone, and the small syllable inventory makes homophony pervasive, which the logographic script (one character per syllable and morpheme, simplified and traditional) disambiguates. It lacks articles, gender, case, agreement, tense and inflectional moods, and its vocabulary splits several concepts into separate words — kinship by lineage and relative age, ‘or’ in questions vs statements, ‘two’ before measure words, ‘can’, ‘know’, ‘wear’, ‘play’, ‘carry’, ‘cut’ — and is rich in compounds, chengyu and culturally loaded homophones.

phenomena.title: Characters: one syllable, one morpheme
phenomena.what: Chinese is written with characters (汉字 hànzì), not letters: each character stands for one spoken syllable and, as a rule, one morpheme (a unit of meaning). A word is one or more characters (书 ‘book’, 学生 ‘student’). The sound is not spelled out, so every character is learned with its reading; about 3,500 common characters cover more than 99 % of everyday texts.

examples.text: 书 · 学生 · 西红柿

phenomena.title: Components and radicals (phono-semantic characters)
phenomena.what: Most characters are built from a meaning part (the radical, e.g. 女 ‘woman’, 口 ‘mouth’, 氵 ‘water’) and a sound part that hints at the reading. Knowing the components makes characters memorable and is how paper dictionaries are ordered. The hint is often only approximate because sounds have changed over 3,000 years.

phenomena.title: Strokes and stroke order
phenomena.what: Characters are written with a fixed set of strokes in a fixed order: top before bottom, left before right, horizontal before vertical, left-falling before right-falling, outside before inside, and a box is closed last. The order matters for handwriting, for handwriting input on phones and for counting strokes (dictionary order).

phenomena.title: Simplified and traditional characters
phenomena.what: Since the 1950s mainland China and Singapore write simplified characters, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau traditional ones. Many common characters differ (书 / 書, 车 / 車, 学 / 學), many do not (人, 大, 好). The words and the grammar are the same; a learner reads one set and recognizes the other.

phenomena.title: One simplified character for several traditional ones
phenomena.what: Simplification often merged two or more characters into one, so one simplified character can have different traditional spellings by meaning: 里 ‘inside’ is 裡 but 里 ‘li (half a kilometre)’ stays 里; 面 ‘face’ is 面 but 面 in 面包 ‘bread’ is 麵. A word with such a character may need a traditional form per sense.

phenomena.title: No spaces between words
phenomena.what: Chinese text has no spaces: characters follow each other and the reader finds the word boundaries. Learners must segment (我 | 喜欢 | 吃 | 西红柿) and some strings can be cut in two ways. Pinyin, in contrast, writes words separately.

phenomena.title: Full-width punctuation, the enumeration comma 、 and book-title marks
phenomena.alsoNote: Japanese also uses full-width 。 and 、, but 、 is its ordinary comma and titles take 『 』.
phenomena.what: Chinese uses full-width punctuation: the small circle 。 as full stop, ，for a comma between clauses, the enumeration comma 、 between items of a list, “ ” for quotes and 《 》 for titles of books and films. The question mark and the exclamation mark are full-width too (？！).

phenomena.title: Horizontal and vertical writing
phenomena.what: Modern Chinese is written left to right in horizontal lines. Traditional books, and still some newspapers and novels in Taiwan and Hong Kong, are set in vertical columns read top to bottom, right to left.

phenomena.title: Two numeral systems and banker's numerals
phenomena.what: Chinese writes numbers with Arabic digits (2026年) or with characters (二〇二六年); prices, dates and phone numbers are mostly in digits, while words like 十一月 or 第一 use characters. On cheques and invoices fraud-proof ‘financial’ characters replace the simple ones (壹 for 一, 贰 for 二, 叁 for 三).

examples.text: 2026年10月8日 = 二〇二六年十月八日
examples.translit: èr líng èr liù nián shí yuè bā rì

phenomena.title: Pinyin: letters with their own values
phenomena.alsoNote: Cantonese is romanized with Jyutping, whose letter values differ; mainland Cantonese speakers usually learned Pinyin at school.
phenomena.what: Hanyu Pinyin writes Mandarin in Latin letters with tone marks. Several letters have values of their own: q = [tɕʰ], x = [ɕ], j = [tɕ], zh / ch / sh / r are retroflex, c = [tsʰ], z = [ts]; ü is written u after j, q, x, y; iou, uei, uen shorten to iu, ui, un after a consonant; i, u, ü at the start of a syllable are written y-, w-, yu-.

phenomena.title: Pinyin word spelling: joined words, apostrophe, capitals
phenomena.what: Pinyin orthography writes the syllables of one word together (wǒmen, xuésheng) and separates words. When a syllable starting with a, o or e follows another syllable inside a word, an apostrophe marks the boundary (Xī'ān, nǚ'ér), otherwise the reading is ambiguous. Proper names and the first word of a sentence are capitalized.

examples.text: 晚安 · 女儿 · 莲藕

phenomena.title: Homophones told apart only in writing
phenomena.what: Because Mandarin has few distinct syllables, many words and morphemes sound the same and are distinguished only by their characters (and by context). 他, 她 and 它 are all tā; 是, 事, 市 and 试 are all shì. Reading and typing therefore mean choosing the right character for the sound.

examples.text: 是 · 事 · 市 · 试
examples.note: to be · matter · city · to try

phenomena.title: No capital letters
phenomena.what: Characters have no capital and small forms: proper names, the first word of a sentence and nouns look like every other word, and names are recognised from context. Only the pinyin romanization uses capitals (Wáng Xiǎomíng, Běijīng).

phenomena.title: One shape per character, wherever it stands
phenomena.what: A character has the same shape at the start, in the middle and at the end of a word or sentence, and printed characters are never joined: each fills its own square. Only handwriting (running and cursive script) links strokes within and between characters.

examples.note: learn · student · university — the same 学 first or last in the word

model.other: fn.overview comparison notes (D18) for ar, fa, he, el: characters never join or change shape, no final forms

phenomena.title: Characters with several readings (多音字)
phenomena.what: Many characters have two or more readings, each tied to a meaning or a word: 行 is xíng in 旅行 ‘travel’ but háng in 银行 ‘bank’; 长 is cháng ‘long’ but zhǎng ‘to grow; chief’. The reading belongs to the word, not to the character, so it must be learned per word and per sense.

phenomena.title: Four lexical tones
phenomena.what: Every Mandarin syllable carries a tone, a pitch contour that distinguishes words: high level (1), rising (2), low dipping (3), falling (4), plus a toneless neutral tone. The same syllable with another tone is another word (买 mǎi ‘buy’, 卖 mài ‘sell’). Because pitch belongs to each word, it is part of every word's dictionary form, and intonation (question, emotion) works on top of the tones without replacing them.

examples.text: 妈 · 麻 · 马 · 骂

phenomena.title: Neutral (light) tone
phenomena.alsoNote: Burmese has toneless reduced (minor) syllables, a related but different phenomenon.
phenomena.what: Some syllables lose their tone and are said short and light: grammatical particles (吗, 了, 们), the suffix 子 and the second syllable of many words. Sometimes the neutral tone alone separates two words. Taiwan Mandarin uses the neutral tone far less (學生 xuéshēng).

phenomena.title: Third-tone sandhi
phenomena.what: A third tone before another third tone is said as a second tone; dictionaries and pinyin keep the written third tone. Before tones 1, 2, 4 and the neutral tone only the low part of the third tone is said.

phenomena.title: Tone changes of 一 and 不
phenomena.what: 不 bù becomes bú before a fourth tone (不是 bú shì). 一 yī becomes yí before a fourth tone (一个 yí ge), yì before tones 1, 2 and 3 (一本 yì běn), and stays yī when counting, at the end and in ordinals (十一, 第一, 一月). Textbooks usually print these spoken tones; dictionaries print yī and bù.

examples.text: 一个 · 一本 · 第一

phenomena.title: Erhua (the -r suffix)
phenomena.what: In northern Mandarin, and above all in Beijing, many words take a rhotic -r (written 儿) that merges with the syllable: 这儿 zhèr, 哪儿 nǎr, 一点儿 yìdiǎnr. Mostly it is a regional or colloquial variant; in some words it changes the meaning (头 tóu ‘head’, 头儿 tóur ‘boss’). Southern speakers and Taiwan mostly say 这里, 哪里, 一点.

phenomena.title: Aspirated and unaspirated stops
phenomena.what: The stops and affricates come in pairs that differ only by aspiration: b, d, g, z, zh, j are voiceless and unaspirated; p, t, k, c, ch, q are the same sounds with a strong puff of air. Voicing does not distinguish them: b, d, g are not voiced. Voicing is distinctive only among the continuants (r [ʐ] vs sh [ʂ]).

phenomena.gap: A pronunciation block in fn.tones / S00 and audio minimal pairs (P9).

phenomena.title: Three series of sibilants: retroflex, alveolo-palatal, dental
phenomena.alsoNote: Serbian distinguishes retroflex and alveolo-palatal affricates (č / ć, dž / đ), but not three full series.
phenomena.what: Mandarin distinguishes zh ch sh r (tongue tip curled back, retroflex), j q x (tongue blade at the hard palate, alveolo-palatal) and z c s (tongue tip at the teeth, dental). Mixing them changes the word (知 zhī ‘know’, 鸡 jī ‘chicken’, 资 zī ‘capital’).

phenomena.title: Apical vowel, ü and the vowel e
phenomena.alsoNote: Albanian has the front rounded y [y], but not the apical vowel or [ɤ].
phenomena.what: The i after z c s and zh ch sh r is not [i] but a buzzing continuation of the consonant (字 zì, 是 shì, 日 rì). ü is a high front rounded vowel [y] (女 nǚ, 绿 lǜ). Pinyin e alone is a back unrounded vowel [ɤ] (饿 è ‘hungry’).

phenomena.title: A small syllable inventory
phenomena.alsoNote: Cantonese also has a small syllable inventory, but with more finals (-m, -p, -t, -k).
phenomena.what: A Mandarin syllable is (consonant) + (glide) + vowel + (n / ng): no consonant clusters and no other final consonants. There are only about 400 syllables (about 1,300 with tones). This explains the many homophones, the preference for two-syllable words, and how loanwords are adapted (final consonants dropped or given a vowel).

examples.note: salad · sofa — no final d, no clusters

phenomena.title: No lexical stress, nothing to mark
phenomena.what: Words have no distinctive lexical stress: what makes a syllable prominent or weak is its tone, and the weak syllables are the toneless neutral-tone ones (东西 dōngxi ‘thing’ vs 东西 dōngxī ‘east and west’). Neither characters nor pinyin have a stress mark, because there is no stress to mark; emphasis on a word in a sentence is given by a wider pitch range and more length.

examples.note: ‘thing’ · ‘east and west’ — told apart by the neutral tone, not by a stress

model.other: fn.tones comparison notes (D18) for the stress languages (el, ru, es, en, de, he, fi, hu, sw …) and the overview note for ru: Mandarin has no word stress, tone does that work

phenomena.title: No distinctive vowel length
phenomena.what: Vowel length never distinguishes words. A syllable sounds longer or shorter because of its tone (a full third tone is long, a neutral-tone syllable short) and its place in the phrase, not because of a long or short vowel.

examples.note: horse (long, low dipping tone) · question particle (short, toneless) — the tone, not a vowel length, makes the difference

model.other: fn.tones comparison notes (D18) for de, hi, ar, ja, fi, hu, lg, iu and the overview notes for ar, fi, hu: length never tells words apart

phenomena.title: No vowel harmony
phenomena.what: Vowels inside a word do not assimilate to each other: every syllable keeps its own vowel, and suffixes and particles have one form after any word (们, 了, 吗 never adapt to the vowels before them).

examples.text: 我们 · 朋友们 · 老师们
examples.note: we · friends · teachers — 们 is the same after any vowel

model.other: fn.overview comparison notes (D18) for tr, fi, hu: particles and suffixes never adapt to vowel harmony (吗 is always 吗)

phenomena.title: No uvular consonants
phenomena.what: No consonant is made at the uvula. h is a velar fricative [x], made at the soft palate, and pinyin q is not a uvular stop but the aspirated alveolo-palatal affricate [tɕʰ].

examples.note: good · go — velar h, palatal q; nothing further back

phenomena.title: No pharyngeal or emphatic consonants
phenomena.what: No consonant is made by narrowing the throat, and there are no pharyngealised (‘emphatic’) consonants: consonants differ by place, aspiration and retroflexion only.

examples.note: drink · big · he — no throat constriction anywhere

model.other: fn.overview comparison note (D18) for ar: pharyngeal and emphatic consonants play no role

phenomena.title: No ejectives or implosives
phenomena.what: Stops differ only by aspiration (b / p, d / t, g / k), never by a closed glottis (ejectives) or by drawing air inwards (implosives).

phenomena.title: No click consonants
phenomena.what: No word contains a click. Clicking noises exist only outside language (tutting in disapproval), and when written they are spelt with ordinary syllables.

phenomena.gap: Not said; a line in the pronunciation table of S00.

phenomena.title: No nasal vowels: -n and -ng are consonants
phenomena.what: There are no nasal vowels. The syllable finals -n and -ng are full consonants that distinguish words (山 shān ‘mountain’ / 伤 shāng ‘wound’); the vowel before them is only slightly nasalised and the consonant itself must be said.

phenomena.title: No final devoicing: only -n, -ng (and -r) end a syllable
phenomena.what: Final devoicing has nothing to act on: a syllable ends in a vowel, -n, -ng or the erhua -r, never in a stop or fricative, and stops do not contrast in voicing anywhere.

examples.note: difficult · busy · where — the only possible syllable ends

model.other: fn.overview comparison notes (D18) for de, ru, tr: syllables end only in a vowel, -n, -ng or -r — nothing to devoice

phenomena.title: No long (double) consonants
phenomena.what: Consonant length never distinguishes words. The only ‘double’ letters in pinyin arise where a syllable ending in -n meets one beginning with n- (安宁 ānníng ‘peaceful’); they belong to two syllables, and no pair of words differs by a single vs a long consonant.

phenomena.title: No ‘th’ sounds
phenomena.what: There are no interdental fricatives [θ ð]: the dental series z c s is made with the tongue tip behind the upper teeth, not between them. Foreign names with such sounds are adapted, usually with s or t.

model.other: fn.overview comparison notes (D18) for el, en, es, ar, sw: no ‘th’ sounds

phenomena.title: l and r: two different sounds
phenomena.what: l and r distinguish words. l is a lateral [l]; pinyin r at the start of a syllable is a retroflex continuant [ʐ ~ ɻ], made with the tongue tip curled back, not a trill or tap. At the end of a syllable r occurs only in 二 èr and as the erhua suffix (哪儿 nǎr).

phenomena.title: No hard / soft consonant pairs
phenomena.what: Consonants do not come in plain / palatalised pairs. The alveolo-palatal j q x are separate consonants that occur only before i and ü, where g k h, z c s and zh ch sh never stand with a real [i] or [y]; so no word changes by ‘softening’ a consonant.

examples.note: chicken · seven · west — j q x before i; *gī, *kī, *hī do not exist

phenomena.title: No consonant mutation
phenomena.what: Initial and final consonants never change with the grammatical context or the word before: a word keeps its consonants everywhere. The systematic sound changes are tonal (third-tone sandhi, 一 and 不) and the erhua -r.

examples.text: 书 · 一本书 · 我的书

phenomena.title: No inflection at all
phenomena.what: Chinese words never change their form: no conjugation for person, number or tense, no plural endings, no cases, no gender, no agreement, no stem changes. 我 is both ‘I’ and ‘me’, 吃 is ‘eat, eats, ate’. Grammar lives in word order and in separate small words.

examples.text: 我吃 · 他吃 · 他们吃
examples.translit: wǒ chī · tā chī · tāmen chī
examples.note: I eat · he eats · they eat

phenomena.title: Words built from morphemes (compounding)
phenomena.what: Most modern words are compounds of two (or more) morphemes, each written with a character: modifier + head (火车 ‘fire-vehicle’ = train), verb + object (开车 ‘drive-car’), verb + result (打破 ‘hit-break’), two parallel members (父母 ‘father-mother’ = parents). Many single morphemes are bound and live only inside compounds (美 in 美食). The parts usually give the meaning away.

examples.text: 火车 · 手机 · 冰箱
examples.note: train (fire + vehicle) · mobile phone (hand + machine) · fridge (ice + box)

phenomena.record: morphemes: the parts of the word with their meanings; the compound type (modifier-head, verb-object, coordinate, verb-result …)

model.other: only free text in etymology

phenomena.gap: A structured morphemes list per word (char + gloss + type), a ‘which parts?’ exercise (like compound_split for German) and word families by shared morpheme.

phenomena.title: Separable verb-object words (离合词)
phenomena.what: Many verbs are a verb + object word (吃饭 ‘eat-rice’, 放假 ‘release-holiday’, 见面 ‘see-face’). Aspect markers, numbers and measure words go between the two parts (吃了饭, 见了一次面), and such a verb cannot take a second direct object — the person goes before it with a coverb (跟他见面 ‘meet him’).

examples.note: to have time off → had three days off

phenomena.title: Noun suffixes 子, 头 and 儿
phenomena.what: Many nouns end in a toneless suffix that adds no meaning but makes a one-syllable morpheme into a two-syllable word: 桌子 ‘table’, 椅子 ‘chair’, 孩子 ‘child’, 木头 ‘wood’, 芋头 ‘taro’. The suffix is dropped inside compounds (饭桌 ‘dining table’).

examples.text: 桌子 · 椅子 · 孩子

model.other: the words are lexemes with neutral-tone pinyin; no morphological analysis

phenomena.gap: A note in fd.04 (most furniture words end in 子) and the morphemes field to mark the suffix.

phenomena.title: 们: a plural only for groups of people
phenomena.what: Nouns have no plural. The suffix 们 makes the plural of pronouns (我们, 你们, 他们) and can mark a definite group of people (孩子们 ‘the children’), but never things and never after a number or 很多.

examples.text: 三个学生（不说 *三个学生们）

phenomena.title: Reduplication
phenomena.what: Doubling is productive: kinship words (妈妈, 哥哥), adverbs (常常 ‘often’), adjectives for vividness (慢慢 ‘slowly’, 高高兴兴 ‘happily’), verbs for ‘a little, briefly’ (看看 ‘have a look’), and nouns or measure words for ‘every’ (人人 ‘everyone’, 天天 ‘every day’). The second syllable of a doubled verb or kin word is toneless.

examples.note: have a look · have a taste

phenomena.title: Word-forming prefixes and suffixes
phenomena.what: A few productive affixes: 老 and 小 before a surname (老王 ‘old Wang’, 小王 ‘young Wang’), 第 before a number for ordinals (第一 ‘first’), 阿 in kin terms (阿姨); agent suffixes 家 (艺术家 ‘artist’), 员 (售货员 ‘shop assistant’), 师 (工程师 ‘engineer’), 者, 手; 们 for groups of people.

examples.text: 艺术家 · 售货员 · 工程师

phenomena.record: morphemes (with the affix marked)

phenomena.title: One word, several parts of speech
phenomena.what: Without endings, the same word often serves as noun, verb or adjective, and only its place shows which: 工作 ‘work’ (noun) and ‘to work’ (verb), 旅行 ‘a trip’ and ‘to travel’, 可能 ‘maybe’, ‘possible’ and ‘possibility’.

examples.note: I work at a bank — verb

phenomena.title: Aspect particles: 了, 过, 着, 在
phenomena.what: Chinese marks how an action is viewed, not when: 了 after the verb for a completed action, 了 at the end for a new situation, 过 for experience (‘have ever’), 在 / 正在 before the verb for an action in progress, 着 for a continuing state. None of them is obligatory: the plain verb also covers ongoing and past events, and time is given by time words.

examples.note: I have been to Beijing — experience
The door is open — continuing state

phenomena.title: No root-and-pattern morphology
phenomena.what: Words are not built from consonant roots filled with vowel patterns: a morpheme is a whole syllable with a fixed vowel and tone, and word families are built by putting such morphemes together.

examples.text: 学 → 学生 · 学校 · 大学
examples.note: learn → student · school · university — the family shares a whole syllable

model.other: fn.overview comparison notes (D18) for ar, he: word families come from compounding whole syllables, not from roots

phenomena.title: No noun incorporation
phenomena.what: Nouns are not absorbed into verbs as affixes. Verb + object words such as 吃饭 ‘eat-rice’ or 睡觉 ‘sleep-sleep’ look similar but stay two words: aspect markers, numbers and modifiers can stand between them (吃了饭, 睡了一个好觉).

examples.text: 睡觉 · 睡了一个好觉
examples.translit: shuìjiào · shuìle yí ge hǎo jiào
examples.note: sleep · had a good sleep — the object part keeps its own measure word and adjective

model.other: fn.overview comparison note (D18) for iu: verb–object words like 吃饭 are separable (吃了饭), not incorporation

phenomena.title: No dual
phenomena.what: Nouns, pronouns and verbs have no dual. ‘Two’ is a numeral + measure word (两个人 ‘two people’), pairs are counted with 双 or 对 (一双鞋 ‘a pair of shoes’), and colloquial 俩 ‘the two of’ follows a pronoun (我们俩 ‘the two of us’).

examples.text: 两个人 · 一双鞋 · 我们俩
examples.translit: liǎng ge rén · yì shuāng xié · wǒmen liǎ
examples.note: two people · a pair of shoes · the two of us

model.other: comparison notes (D18) for ar, iu

phenomena.gap: 双, 对 (pair) and 俩 are not in the course; the absence of a dual is said in the comparison notes for ar and iu (D18: fn.pronoun.subject, fn.numerals, fn.plural.noun).

phenomena.title: No collective / singulative forms: measure words single out one
phenomena.what: A noun has no special form for ‘one piece of’ a mass or a group. One unit is picked out by a measure word, and the noun stays the same: 一粒米 ‘a grain of rice’, 一根头发 ‘a hair’, 一滴水 ‘a drop of water’.
phenomena.gap: Measure words are covered (zh.syntax.measure); unit measures such as 粒 and 滴 and the singling-out use are not taught.

phenomena.title: No grammatical gender or noun classes
phenomena.what: Nouns have no grammatical gender and no noun classes, and nothing agrees with a noun. The sex of a person or animal is said with words: 男 / 女 for people (男老师 ‘male teacher’, 女学生 ‘female student’), 公 / 母 for animals (公鸡 ‘rooster’, 母鸡 ‘hen’), and in writing 他 / 她 / 它. The measure word, not a gender, is what every noun brings with it.

examples.text: 这个男孩 · 这个女孩
examples.note: this boy · this girl — 这个 is the same for both

phenomena.title: No cases
phenomena.what: Nouns and pronouns have no cases and no case particles: the same form is subject, object, possessor and the noun after a coverb (我 ‘I, me’; 我的 ‘my’ is 我 + the particle 的). Roles are shown by word order and by coverbs before the verb (给他 ‘to him’, 从北京 ‘from Beijing’).

examples.translit: Wǒ ài tā. · Tā ài wǒ.
examples.note: I love him. · He loves me. — 我 and 他 do not change; only their place does

phenomena.title: No possessive affixes
phenomena.what: Possession is never marked by an affix on the noun: the possessor is a separate word before it, joined by 的 (我的书 ‘my book’, 老师的书 ‘the teacher’s book’). There are no possessive words of their own; ‘my’ is ‘I’ + 的.

examples.text: 我的书 · 他们的房子
examples.translit: wǒ de shū · tāmen de fángzi

phenomena.title: No subject agreement on the verb
phenomena.what: The verb never agrees with its subject: 我是, 你是, 他是, 我们是, 他们是 — one form for every person and number. Who acts is said by the subject, or understood from context when it is left out.

examples.text: 我吃 · 你吃 · 他们吃
examples.translit: wǒ chī · nǐ chī · tāmen chī
examples.note: I eat · you eat · they eat — 吃 never changes

phenomena.title: No object marking on the verb
phenomena.what: The verb carries no sign of its object — no object agreement, no object pronouns attached to it, no separate conjugation for definite objects. The object is a separate word after the verb (我爱你 ‘I love you’), placed before it with 把 or as a topic, or left out when it is known.

examples.note: I love you. — 你 is a separate word; 爱 is unchanged
I finished reading the book. — the object moved before the verb with 把

phenomena.title: No past tense
phenomena.what: There is no past tense: the verb is the same for past, present and future (我昨天去 / 我今天去 / 我明天去). A past event is placed in time by time words or by context; 了 and 过 mark completion and experience, not past time, and many past sentences have neither (我以前住在北京 ‘I used to live in Beijing’).

examples.note: I went to Beijing yesterday. — the time word alone places it in the past
I used to live in Beijing. — no 了

model.other: fn.past (cr.01): time words + 了 for completion, 没 for negation; bank variants Tense PST

phenomena.title: No future tense
phenomena.what: There is no future tense: the plain verb with a time word is enough (我明天去北京 ‘I’ll go to Beijing tomorrow’). Optional words add intention or likelihood — 要 ‘be going to’, 会 ‘will (probably)’, 打算 ‘plan to’, formal 将 — but none of them is required.

model.other: fn.future (cr.03): time words, 要, 会 (zh:hui.will), 打算 / 计划; bank variants Tense FUT, Polarity, Mood

phenomena.gap: 将 / 将要 (the written future) is named in the page but is not a lexeme of the course.

phenomena.title: The perfect from "finish": sentence-final 了
phenomena.what: There is no perfect verb form (no auxiliary + participle). Current relevance is marked by sentence-final 了, a particle that grew out of 了 liǎo "to finish": a situation has come about and still holds (他来了 "he has come / he is here now"). 过 marks experience ("have ever") and 已经 "already" completion.

examples.note: He has come (and is here now).

model.other: 已经 (zh:yijing, cr.01, role: its concept adv.already is taught in C40) with 已经 … 了 in fn.past

phenomena.gap: fn.past teaches 已经 … 了 and the new-situation 了; the overview does not yet relate sentence-final 了 to ‘current relevance’, and 还没 (not yet) has no lexeme 还.

phenomena.title: No subjunctive
phenomena.what: There is no subjunctive mood: the verb is the same in wishes, purposes, hypotheses and reported or doubted statements. These are marked by words: 希望 ‘hope’, 让 ‘let’, 如果 / 要是 ‘if’, 为了 ‘in order to’.

examples.note: I hope (that) you come. — 来 as in any other sentence

model.other: fn.overview comparison notes (D18) for es, fr

phenomena.gap: 希望 and 为了 are not in the course; the absence is said only in the overview notes for es and fr (D18).

phenomena.title: No particle verbs or preverbs
phenomena.what: There is no class of particle verbs or prefixed verbs. Direction and result are added by full verbs after the main verb (进来 ‘come in’, 拿出来 ‘take out’, 吃完 ‘finish eating’); these are open, regular combinations rather than separate lexical verbs.

examples.text: 拿 · 拿出来 · 拿回去
examples.note: take · take out (towards here) · take back (away from here)

phenomena.gap: Directional and resultative complements are not taught yet (zh.syntax.complement.direction, zh.syntax.complement.result).

phenomena.title: Adjectives never agree
phenomena.what: An adjective has one form before every noun, singular or plural, in any role: 大房子 ‘a big house’, 很多大房子 ‘many big houses’, 大城市 ‘a big city’. Nothing in the adjective refers back to the noun.

examples.text: 大房子 · 很多大房子
examples.translit: dà fángzi · hěn duō dà fángzi
examples.note: a big house · many big houses — 大 never changes

phenomena.title: Fixed SVO order carries the grammar
phenomena.what: With no cases and no agreement, the order subject – verb – object decides who does what. 妈妈喜欢孩子 and 孩子喜欢妈妈 mean different things; the object does not move before the verb in a plain sentence (only with 把 or as a topic).

phenomena.title: Time and place before the verb
phenomena.what: Everything that sets the scene — when and where — stands before the verb: subject – time – place – verb – object. ‘I eat at home tomorrow’ is 我明天在家吃饭; the place and the time never follow the verb in a plain sentence.

examples.note: In the evening we eat at home — time before place

phenomena.title: Point in time before the verb, duration after it
phenomena.what: A point in time (at eight) comes before the verb, but how long something lasts (for eight hours) comes after it. The same time word changes its meaning with its place.

model.other: trap in fn.prep.time

phenomena.gap: The bank now has durations after the verb (睡了八个小时, 等了你半个小时, 待两个星期); still missing: durations with an object (我学了三年中文) and a contrast exercise (when vs how long).

phenomena.title: Topic–comment sentences
phenomena.what: A sentence may open with a topic — what it is about — and then say something about it, even when the topic is the object or has no grammatical role at all. Often the topic is something already known.

examples.note: Elephants have long trunks (elephant – trunk – long).

model.other: fn.word.order mentions a topic opening the sentence

phenomena.gap: Bank sentences with a fronted object or double subject, and a transform ‘make X the topic’.

phenomena.title: Modifiers before the noun, relative clauses with 的
phenomena.what: Everything that describes a noun comes before it, joined by 的: an owner (我的书), an adjective phrase (很大的房子), a whole clause (我昨天买的书 ‘the book I bought yesterday’). There is no relative pronoun; the head noun comes last.

examples.translit: yì běn guānyú jiātíng de shū

model.other: zh:de lexeme (的) with senses

phenomena.gap: Relative clauses (cr.06) are not written yet; the bank has few clause-plus-的 sentences.

phenomena.title: Three particles pronounced de: 的, 得, 地
phenomena.what: Three different particles all sound de and are told apart only in writing: 的 links a modifier to a noun (我的书), 地 links a manner phrase to a verb (慢慢地走 ‘walk slowly’), 得 links a verb to a comment on how it is done (跑得很快 ‘runs fast’). Native writers also mix them up.

model.other: only 的 is a lexeme; 得 appears in a trap of fn.adjective; 地 is not in the course

phenomena.gap: Lexemes for 得 and 地, a function (complement of degree, manner adverbials) and a contrast exercise 的 / 得 / 地.

phenomena.title: Measure words (classifiers)
phenomena.what: A number or 这 / 那 / 哪 / 几 cannot stand directly before a noun: a measure word comes between them, chosen by the kind or shape of the thing — 本 for books, 张 for flat things, 把 for things with a handle, 条 for long things, 位 politely for people, 个 as the general one. Every noun is learned with its measure word.

examples.text: 一本书 · 三张桌子 · 这把椅子
examples.translit: yì běn shū · sān zhāng zhuōzi · zhè bǎ yǐzi
examples.note: a book · three tables · this chair

phenomena.what: Besides sortal classifiers that only count (一本书), containers and units serve as measures (一杯茶 ‘a cup of tea’, 一碗米饭 ‘a bowl of rice’, 一瓶水 ‘a bottle of water’). Mass nouns take only these. A container word as a thing takes its own measure word: 一个杯子 ‘a cup’.

phenomena.title: Verbal measure words (次, 遍, 下)
phenomena.what: Actions are counted with their own measure words after the verb: 次 and 回 for occurrences, 遍 for times through from start to end, 下 for a quick action (一下 softens a request).

examples.note: I have been to Beijing twice.

phenomena.record: kind: verbal on such measure words

phenomena.title: Coverbs: verbs in the role of prepositions
phenomena.what: The words that introduce a place, a source, a companion, a recipient or a standard of comparison (在 ‘at’, 从 ‘from’, 跟 ‘with’, 给 ‘for, to’, 离 ‘from (distance)’, 比 ‘than’) are, or were, verbs. With their noun they stand before the main verb, never after it: ‘I eat at home’ is literally ‘I be-at home eat’ (我在家吃饭).

phenomena.title: Place words after the noun (localizers)
phenomena.alsoNote: Japanese and Korean put relational place nouns after the noun too (机の上 / 책상 위 'on the desk'), and Amharic frames a place with a preposition plus a postposed place noun.
phenomena.what: Where something is inside, on or under is said with a place word after the noun: 桌子上 ‘on the table’, 冰箱里 ‘in the fridge’. An ordinary object noun needs such a place word to be a place (在冰箱里, not *在冰箱), while place names and institutions do not (在学校, 在北京). Together with the coverb 在 before the noun, the place is framed from both sides.

examples.note: The book is on the table.
The milk is in the fridge.
I'm at school — no 里 needed

phenomena.record: place: whether the noun is a place by itself (学校, 医院) or needs 里 / 上 (冰箱, 房间)

phenomena.title: Three ‘to be’: 是, 在, 有 (and none before adjectives)
phenomena.what: Three different words cover being: 是 links two nouns (我是老师), 在 says where someone or something is (老师在这里), 有 says that something exists somewhere (这里有很多人 ‘there are many people here’), and adjectives need no verb at all (我很好).

phenomena.title: Existence: place first, then 有
phenomena.what: ‘There is a book on the table’ starts with the place: 桌子上有一本书. A new, indefinite thing comes after 有; a known thing comes first with 在: 书在桌子上 ‘the book is on the table’. Word order thus shows whether a thing is known or new.

examples.translit: Zhuōzi shang yǒu yì běn shū.
examples.note: There is a book on the table.
The book is on the table.

phenomena.title: Adjectives as predicates with 很
phenomena.what: Adjectives are stative verbs: they are the predicate themselves, with no 是. A plain statement uses an unstressed 很 as a link (这个房子很大); a bare adjective sounds contrastive. Before a noun a one-syllable adjective attaches directly (新书), a longer or modified one takes 的 (很新的书).

examples.translit: xīn shū · hěn xīn de shū
examples.note: a new book · a very new book

model.other: zh:hen with its role

phenomena.title: Two negators: 不 and 没
phenomena.what: 不 negates will, habits, the present and future, adjectives and 是; 没 (有) negates 有 and says that something did not happen or has not happened yet. ‘Don't!’ is 别 or 不要. The negator stands right before the verb (or before 在 + place), and the choice depends on aspect and on the verb, not on tense.
phenomena.record: features.neg on verbs: bu+mei | bu | mei (是 → 不 only, 有 → 没 only)

model.other: zh:bu, zh:mei, zh:bie lexemes; features.neg on every verb; the contrast generator listed in fn.negation is not implemented yet

phenomena.title: Questions with 吗, A-not-A and 呢
phenomena.alsoNote: Vietnamese có … không? frames the verb in a similar way.
phenomena.what: A yes/no question adds the particle 吗 at the end of the statement, or repeats the verb with 不 between (A-not-A: 你喝不喝茶？); nothing moves and the voice need not rise. 呢 asks ‘and …?’ (你呢？ ‘and you?’) or softens a question-word question.

model.other: zh:ma lexeme; bank variant QuestionForm

phenomena.gap: 呢 is not a lexeme of the course (‘and you?’ is basic, S02/S09).

phenomena.title: Question words stay in place
phenomena.what: A question word stands exactly where the answer will stand; nothing is fronted and no 吗 is added. Write the answer, then replace the unknown part.

examples.note: What do you drink? (answer: 我喝茶)
When are you coming? — time before the verb

phenomena.title: Question words as ‘any-, every-, no-’
phenomena.what: The question words double as indefinites: 什么 ‘something, anything’, 谁 ‘anyone’, 哪儿 ‘anywhere’. With 都 / 也 they mean ‘every-’ or, negated, ‘no-’: 我什么都不吃 ‘I eat nothing’, 谁都知道 ‘everybody knows’.

model.other: zh:shenmedou is a lexeme for pron.nothing; senses of 什么 / 谁 / 哪里 list the indefinite uses

phenomena.gap: 什么都 is stored as one word; the general pattern (any question word + 都 / 也) has no function or generator.

phenomena.title: No general ‘yes’ and ‘no’: echo answers
phenomena.alsoNote: Vietnamese often echoes the verb too, but also has general 'yes' words (vâng, dạ) and không 'no'.
phenomena.what: Yes/no questions are answered by repeating the verb (or adjective), negated for ‘no’: 要。/ 不要。, 有。/ 没有。; 对 ‘right’ confirms a statement. 是 means ‘yes’ only for questions with 是.

examples.note: Do you have an elder brother? — No.

model.other: part.yes is realized by 是 and 对 with their senses

phenomena.title: Resultative and potential complements
phenomena.what: A second verb or adjective after the verb says what the action achieved: 看懂 ‘read and understand’, 买到 ‘manage to buy’, 吃完 ‘finish eating’. With 得 / 不 inside, it says whether the result is possible: 听得懂 ‘can understand (by listening)’, 听不懂 ‘cannot understand’. Causing a change is said the same way — 打破 ‘hit-break’ = break (something), 叫醒 ‘call-wake’ = wake (someone up) — or with 让 / 使 ‘make, let’ before a clause.
phenomena.record: results: the result complements a verb typically takes (懂, 到, 完, 好)

model.other: only sense texts (到 s4 ‘managed to’, 不 s3 ‘cannot’)

phenomena.gap: A grammar function, lexemes 懂, 完, 见, and bank sentences; 睡着 (cr.01) and 长大 (cr.02) are stored as whole words with a note on their result part.

phenomena.title: Directional complements with 来 / 去
phenomena.what: Movement verbs take 来 (towards the speaker) or 去 (away from the speaker) after them, often with a path verb 上, 下, 进, 出, 回, 过 in between: 进来 ‘come in’, 出去 ‘go out’, 跑进来 ‘run in’, 拿回来 ‘bring back’. Manner, path and deixis are all verbs of equal rank, and the deixis (towards / away from here) is expressed whenever movement is described.
phenomena.record: directions: the directional complements a verb takes

model.other: senses of 来, 去, 回, 回来, 进, 出 list the complement uses; 回来 is a lexeme

phenomena.gap: A function for compound directionals (V + 进 / 出 / 回 … + 来 / 去) with the object position rule, and generators.

phenomena.title: Complement of degree with 得
phenomena.what: How well or how fast something is done follows the verb with 得: 他跑得很快 ‘he runs fast’. With an object the verb is repeated (or the object fronted): 他说中文说得很好 / 他中文说得很好 ‘he speaks Chinese well’.

examples.translit: Tā shuō Zhōngwén shuō de hěn hǎo.

model.other: a trap of fn.adjective (*他跑很快 → 他跑得很快)

phenomena.gap: Lexeme 得 (de), a function with the verb-copy rule and bank sentences.

phenomena.title: The 把 construction
phenomena.alsoNote: Cantonese has a similar but much rarer, formal 將 construction.
phenomena.what: With 把 the definite object moves before the verb, and the sentence says what is done to it and with what result: 我把书放在桌子上了 ‘I put the book on the table’. The verb must be followed by something (a place, a result, 了). It is required with verbs like 放 ‘put’ when the place follows.

examples.translit: Wǒ bǎ shū fàng zài zhuōzi shang le.
examples.note: I put the book on the table.

model.other: 把 exists only as the measure word for handled things (zh:ba, CLF)

phenomena.gap: A 把 lexeme (ADP, disposal), a function (after resultative and directional complements), bank sentences and a transform 把 ↔ plain SVO.

phenomena.title: The 被 passive
phenomena.alsoNote: Cantonese 畀 passive has the same structure but is used for neutral events too; Japanese has an adversative passive in -(r)are-.
phenomena.what: 被 marks the passive: object – 被 – (agent) – verb – result. It is used mainly for unwelcome events (stolen, broken, criticised); for neutral events Chinese prefers an active sentence or a topic. Like 把, the verb needs something after it.

examples.translit: Wǒ de qiánbāo bèi tōu le.

examples.note: He was criticised by the teacher.

model.other: nothing

phenomena.gap: Lexeme 被, a function with the ‘adversative’ use and a transform active ↔ 被.

phenomena.title: Serial verbs
phenomena.what: Two or more verb phrases follow each other without a conjunction, in the order of events or purpose: 坐公共汽车去学校 ‘go to school by bus’ (sit-bus go-school), 去买菜 ‘go and buy vegetables’, 来一杯咖啡.

examples.translit: Wǒ zuò gōnggòng qìchē qù xuéxiào.
examples.note: I go to school by bus.
We go to the supermarket to buy things.

model.other: 坐 and 骑 lexemes with roles; trap *我去学校坐公共汽车

phenomena.gap: The general pattern (purpose, means) as a grammar point; now only the transport case of fd.13.

phenomena.title: Pivot verbs: 请, 叫, 让
phenomena.what: In 我请他吃饭 ‘I invite him to eat’ the person is the object of the first verb and the subject of the second. Verbs of asking, inviting, ordering and letting (请, 叫, 让) work this way.

examples.note: I'm inviting him for a meal.
Mum tells me to come home.

phenomena.record: frame: the pivot frame (V + person + V) on the verb

model.other: senses of 请 and 叫 mention it; 让 is not in the course

phenomena.gap: A function with the causatives (cr.39) and bank sentences; 让 as a lexeme.

phenomena.title: Focus with 是……的
phenomena.what: For a past event already known, 是……的 puts the focus on when, where, how or with whom it happened: 你是怎么来的？ ‘how did you come?’ — 我是坐飞机来的 ‘I came by plane’. It is the normal way to ask about the circumstances of a past event.

examples.translit: Wǒ shì zuò fēijī lái de.

model.other: 是 sense s3 names the construction

phenomena.gap: Not taught yet: fn.past (cr.01) only points to 是…的 for the circumstances of a past event (你几点睡的？); the common plan puts it with emphasis in C43, although learners meet it from A2.

phenomena.title: Sentence-final particles
phenomena.what: Small toneless particles at the end of a sentence add mood: 吗 (question), 吧 (suggestion, guess), 呢 (‘and …?’, ongoing), 了 (new situation), 啊 (warmth, emphasis). Since pitch is taken by the lexical tones, much of the attitude of a sentence is carried by these particles.
phenomena.record: features.position on PART: afterVerb | sentenceFinal | clauseFinal | afterModifier | afterNoun

model.other: 吗, 吧, 了, 过, 的, 们, 的话 are lexemes with features.position

phenomena.gap: 呢 and 啊 are missing; no overview of the particles as a system.

phenomena.title: Dropping known subjects and objects
phenomena.what: Anything clear from context can be left out — the subject and also the object — although the verb has no endings to recover them: ‘Have you eaten?’ is just 吃了吗？, and the answer 吃了。 What is left out is understood from the situation and the previous sentences.

examples.note: — Do you know him? — Yes (I know him).

model.other: echo answers in the bank

phenomena.gap: A short explanation and bank dialogues with dropped objects; production exercises that accept the dropped forms (alts).

phenomena.title: Comparison with 比, 没有, 一样
phenomena.what: The adjective never changes: A 比 B + adjective (我哥哥比我高), the difference after it (高一点, 大两岁), ‘not as … as’ A 没有 B + adjective, ‘as … as’ A 跟 B 一样 + adjective; 最 for ‘the most’. No 很 inside a comparison.

examples.note: My elder brother is taller than me.
I'm not as tall as him.

phenomena.title: Paired connectives and clause-final ‘when’ / ‘if’
phenomena.alsoNote: Vietnamese pairs its connectives the same way (vì … nên, tuy … nhưng, nếu … thì); Japanese marks 'when' and 'if' at the end of the clause (…時, …なら).
phenomena.what: Clauses are often linked by pairs: 因为…所以 ‘because … so’, 虽然…但是 ‘although … but’, 如果…就 ‘if … then’. ‘When’ and ‘if’ can be marked at the end of their clause (…的时候, …的话). ‘And’ (和) never joins clauses.

examples.translit: Suīrán hěn guì, dànshì hěn hǎo.
Wǒ è de shíhou chī miànbāo.
examples.note: When I'm hungry I eat bread.

phenomena.record: features.pair on SCONJ: the partner word of the paired construction (因为 → 所以, 虽然 → 但是 / 可是, 如果 → 就)

phenomena.title: Adverbs before the verb: 都, 也, 只, 就, 才
phenomena.what: Adverbs stand right before the verb (or before 在 + place), never at the end or before the subject: 我们都喝茶. 都 sums up what stands before it (我们都 ‘we all’). 就 says ‘as early as / then’, 才 ‘only then, as late as’: the pair shows whether something happens earlier or later than expected.

examples.text: 他八点就来了。 · 他十点才来。
examples.translit: Tā bā diǎn jiù lái le. · Tā shí diǎn cái lái.
examples.note: He came already at eight. · He only came at ten.

phenomena.record: features.position on ADV: preverbal | sentenceInitial | afterVerb

model.other: every adverb states where it stands; 就 is a lexeme with role; traps *都我们

phenomena.gap: 才 is not in the course; the 就 / 才 contrast needs a function with bank sentences.

phenomena.title: Modal verbs: 会, 能, 可以, 要, 想, 应该
phenomena.what: ‘Can’ splits by its source: 会 a learned skill (我会说中文), 能 ability or circumstances (我今天不能来), 可以 permission (这里可以坐吗？). ‘Want’ splits into 要 (will, demand) and 想 (would like). Modals stand before the main verb, which is the same plain form as everywhere else (there is no infinitive), and neither changes.

examples.note: I can speak Chinese (have learned it).

model.other: 要 and 想 exist (verb.want); 会 exists from cr.03 (zh:hui.will, senses ‘will’ and ‘can’); 能, 可以, 应该 not yet

phenomena.gap: Lexemes 能, 可以, 应该 and a realization of fn.modal (cr.05) with the 会 / 能 / 可以 decision procedure.

phenomena.title: No definite article
phenomena.what: There is no definite article. Whether a noun is known is shown by its place (a bare noun before the verb is usually known: 书在桌子上 ‘the book is on the table’), by 这 / 那 + measure word, or by the context; a new thing usually stands after the verb (桌子上有一本书 ‘there is a book on the table’).

examples.note: The book is on the table. — known: a bare noun before the verb

phenomena.title: 一 + measure word as ‘a’
phenomena.what: One newly introduced thing can be marked with the numeral 一 ‘one’ + measure word, which works as an indefinite ‘a’: 我买了一本书 ‘I bought a book’. After a verb 一 is often dropped in speech (买了本书), and with a non-specific noun, especially after 是, nothing is used (我是老师 ‘I am a teacher’).

examples.note: I am a teacher. — no 一

phenomena.title: No grammatical classes of possession
phenomena.what: Possession is not split into grammatical classes (alienable / inalienable, or by kind of possessed thing). Leaving out 的 with kin terms, one’s home and institutions (我妈妈 ‘my mother’, 我家 ‘my family, my home’, 我们公司 ‘our company’) is a tendency of closeness and style, not an obligatory class: 我的妈妈 is also correct.

examples.text: 我妈妈 · 我的妈妈 · 我的书
examples.translit: wǒ māma · wǒ de māma · wǒ de shū
examples.note: my mother (both correct) · my book (的 needed)

phenomena.gap: fn.possessive explains when 的 is dropped but not that this is optional style rather than a class of nouns.

phenomena.title: The possessed noun never changes
phenomena.what: The possessed or modified noun keeps its form, and there is no construct form, ezafe or linking suffix on it: the link 的 follows the possessor or modifier (老师的书 ‘the teacher’s book’), and the head noun comes last, unchanged.

examples.text: 书 · 老师的书 · 很新的书
examples.translit: shū · lǎoshī de shū · hěn xīn de shū
examples.note: book · the teacher’s book · a very new book — 书 never changes

model.other: fn.possessive comparison notes (D18) for ar, he (construct state) and fa (ezafe): the possessed noun never changes, only the owner takes 的

phenomena.title: Conditions by conjunctions only
phenomena.what: Conditions are marked only by conjunctions and adverbs, and the verb is unchanged: 如果 / 要是 ‘if’ opens the clause, …的话 can close it, and 就 introduces the result. Real and unreal (counterfactual) conditions look the same; the context, or words such as 早知道 ‘had I known’, show which is meant.

examples.text: 如果明天下雨，我们就不去。
examples.translit: Rúguǒ míngtiān xià yǔ, wǒmen jiù bú qù.
examples.note: If it rains tomorrow, we won’t go.

examples.translit: Zǎo zhīdao, wǒ jiù bù lái le.
examples.note: Had I known, I wouldn’t have come. — the same verb forms

phenomena.title: No grammatical evidentials
phenomena.what: The verb does not mark the source of information. When it matters, words say it: 听说 ‘I hear that’, 据说 ‘reportedly’, 好像 ‘it seems’, 看来 ‘it looks as if’.

examples.note: I hear he is ill. — hearsay said with a verb
He is ill. — the same sentence without a source

model.other: fn.overview comparison note (D18) for tr

phenomena.gap: 听说 and 好像 are not in the course; the absence is said only in the overview note for tr (D18).

phenomena.title: No antipassive
phenomena.what: There is no antipassive voice. When the object does not matter, the verb is used with a general object in a verb-object word (我在吃饭 ‘I’m eating’, 他在看书 ‘he’s reading’) or the object is simply left out; the verb never changes.

examples.note: I’m eating. — a general object 饭 rather than a special verb form

phenomena.gap: Not said; the verb-object words of zh.morph.separable show the pattern.

phenomena.title: No applicative: coverbs add participants
phenomena.what: No affix on the verb adds a beneficiary, recipient or companion. They are introduced by a coverb before the verb (给妈妈打电话 ‘phone Mum’, 为你高兴 ‘happy for you’, 跟朋友去 ‘go with friends’) or by 给 after a verb of giving (送给他 ‘give to him’).

examples.note: I phone Mum. — 给 + person before the verb

phenomena.gap: Coverbs are taught (fn.prep.core); verb + 给 (送给, 借给) is not.

phenomena.title: No converbs: clauses chained by sequence
phenomena.what: Verbs have no dependent forms meaning ‘while / after / by doing’. Actions are chained by placing verb phrases one after another (serial verbs), by 着 for an accompanying state (笑着说 ‘said smiling’), or by a time word after the clause (吃饭以后 ‘after eating’).

examples.note: After eating we go to the park.

phenomena.gap: 以后 after a clause (fn.prep.time), V1 了 … 就 V2 (fn.past) and V1 着 V2 (fn.past.ongoing: 他坐着等我) are taught; the general picture of clause chaining waits for C19 (fn.sequence).

phenomena.title: No participles: a clause + 的 instead
phenomena.what: The verb has no adjectival forms. A verb phrase or clause before 的 does the work: 在跑的人 ‘the running man’, 昨天买的书 ‘the book bought yesterday’, 会说中文的人 ‘people who speak Chinese’.
phenomena.gap: Relative clauses with 的 (cr.06) are not written yet.

phenomena.title: No verb-second rule
phenomena.what: The verb has no fixed second position: a time word or adverb at the start does not move it (明天我去 and 我明天去 ‘tomorrow I go’ — the subject still comes before the verb), and main and subordinate clauses have the same order.

examples.text: 明天我去北京。· 我明天去北京。
examples.translit: Míngtiān wǒ qù Běijīng. · Wǒ míngtiān qù Běijīng.
examples.note: Tomorrow I go to Beijing. — both orders keep subject before verb

model.other: fn.word.order (block German V2 vs Chinese) and comparison notes (D18) for de in fn.word.order, fn.time.day and fn.overview

phenomena.title: 有: ‘have’ and ‘there is’ in one verb
phenomena.what: One verb 有 serves for both possession and existence. With a person first it is ‘have’ (我有一个哥哥 ‘I have an elder brother’); with a place or time first it is ‘there is’ (这里有很多人 ‘there are many people here’). The possessor is simply the first noun — the topic — of an existential sentence. 有 never changes and is negated only with 没 (没有).

phenomena.title: No switch-reference
phenomena.what: Nothing on the verb shows whether the next clause has the same subject or a different one. The subject is repeated when it changes and left out when it stays the same.

examples.translit: Tā chīwán fàn jiù zǒu le.
Tā chīwán fàn wǒ jiù zǒu le.
examples.note: He finished eating and then I left. — the new subject is simply named

phenomena.gap: Not said; a line in the connectors block (fn.connectors).

phenomena.title: Kinship terms by lineage, age and sex
phenomena.alsoNote: Korean, Vietnamese and Hindi also split uncles and aunts by side and by relative age, with their own sets of terms.
phenomena.what: Chinese has no general ‘uncle’, ‘aunt’, ‘cousin’ or ‘grandfather’: the word says whose side (father's or mother's), older or younger, and blood relative or in-law. 叔叔 is the father's younger brother, 伯伯 his elder brother, 舅舅 the mother's brother; 堂 cousins are the children of the father's brothers, all others are 表.

examples.text: 叔叔 · 伯伯 · 舅舅
examples.note: father's younger brother · father's elder brother · mother's brother
elder male cousin on the father's brothers' side · on any other side

phenomena.record: kin: lineage (paternal / maternal), relative age (elder / younger), sex, blood / in-law

model.other: fd.06 has all the terms as separate lexemes of the same concept; contrasts give each word its value on one axis per concept (side, relative age, blood / in-law)

phenomena.gap: A structured kin field (lineage, age, sex, in-law) is not declared, so no sense_split / kin-tree exercise can ask ‘your mother’s brother?’; no family-tree picture.

phenomena.title: Elder and younger siblings are different words
phenomena.what: Everyday Chinese has no neutral word for ‘brother’ or ‘sister’: it is 哥哥 (elder) or 弟弟 (younger), 姐姐 or 妹妹. 兄弟 and 姐妹 mean ‘brothers’ / ‘sisters’ as a group.

examples.text: 我有一个哥哥和两个妹妹。
examples.translit: Wǒ yǒu yí ge gēge hé liǎng ge mèimei.
examples.note: I have an elder brother and two younger sisters.

phenomena.record: kin.age: elder | younger

model.other: four lexemes for family.brother / family.sister; contrasts on the axis ‘relative age’

phenomena.gap: The kin field is not declared; no exercise forces the choice (‘your younger brother’).

phenomena.title: Kin terms for strangers
phenomena.what: Kin words are used to address people who are not relatives, by their age relative to the speaker: children call adults 叔叔 ‘uncle’ and 阿姨 ‘auntie’, young people call a slightly older woman 姐姐 or 大姐, an old man is 爷爷 or 大爷, a child is 小朋友 ‘little friend’.

examples.note: Auntie, how much is this? (to a middle-aged saleswoman)
How old are you, little one?

phenomena.record: address: the address use of a kin noun (as a sense with register)

model.other: senses ‘a friendly address for …’ on 叔叔, 阿姨, 姐姐, 弟弟, 爷爷, 奶奶

phenomena.gap: An address register on these senses and a register / dialogue_turn exercise (who would you call 阿姨?).

phenomena.title: Address by title and surname
phenomena.what: People are addressed by surname + title or job (王老师 ‘Teacher Wang’, 李医生 ‘Dr Li’), or among acquaintances by 老 / 小 + surname (老王, 小李). Using the given name alone is intimate; using 你 to a teacher instead of the title sounds rude.

examples.note: Xiao Li, come here a moment.

model.other: senses of 老师 (title), 老 / 小 (prefixes); fn.greetings mentions 老师好

phenomena.gap: A pragmatics block (titles, surname-first names) and dialogue exercises.

phenomena.title: Polite 您 and familiar 你
phenomena.what: 您 is the respectful ‘you’ for elders, teachers, customers and strangers to be honoured; 你 is used between equals and towards strangers in everyday situations without sounding rude. 您 is singular only (the plural is 你们 or, very formally, 各位), and the verb never changes.
phenomena.record: register: honorific on 您

model.other: zh:nin and zh:ninhao lexemes; bank variant Formality

phenomena.title: Inclusive 咱们
phenomena.what: Beside 我们 ‘we’ there is 咱们 ‘we, you and I together’, which always includes the listener (northern, colloquial). 我们 can exclude the listener in the north but is used for both in the south.

model.other: zh:zanmen lexeme with a trap in fn.pronoun.subject

phenomena.title: One tā, three characters
phenomena.what: ‘He’, ‘she’ and ‘it’ are all tā in speech; only writing distinguishes 他, 她 and 它 (a 20th-century innovation). In speech the third-person pronoun shows no gender.

examples.text: 他们 · 她们 · 它们

model.other: separate lexemes; traps note the same sound

phenomena.title: Two words for ‘or’: 还是 and 或者
phenomena.what: In a question offering a choice, ‘or’ is 还是 (and no 吗); in statements it is 或者. The two are not interchangeable.

examples.note: Do you drink tea or coffee?

examples.text: 我喝茶或者咖啡都可以。
examples.translit: Wǒ hē chá huòzhě kāfēi dōu kěyǐ.
examples.note: Tea or coffee, either is fine for me.

model.other: two lexemes for conj.or

phenomena.title: Riding: 坐 (sit in) vs 骑 (sit astride)
phenomena.alsoNote: Cantonese pedals a bicycle (踩單車) rather than sitting astride it.
phenomena.what: ‘Go by’ a vehicle depends on how you sit: 坐 for vehicles you sit in as a passenger (bus, train, plane, taxi, boat), 骑 for what you straddle (bicycle, motorbike, horse); driving yourself is 开.

examples.text: 坐公共汽车 · 坐飞机

phenomena.record: per vehicle noun: the verb used to travel by it (坐 / 骑 / 开)

model.other: zh:zuo, zh:qi.ride lexemes; trap *我坐自行车

phenomena.title: ‘Know’: 知道, 认识, 会
phenomena.what: ‘To know’ splits three ways: 知道 a fact, 认识 a person or place (also ‘recognize’), 会 a skill learned (‘know how to’).

model.other: 认识 only inside the fixed phrase 认识你很高兴; none is a lexeme

phenomena.gap: Concepts and lexemes (know a fact / know a person / know how) and a sense_split exercise — a basic early verb set.

phenomena.title: ‘Wear’: 穿 vs 戴
phenomena.what: 穿 is for what you put your body into (clothes, shoes, socks), 戴 for what you put on or attach (hat, glasses, watch, gloves, jewellery, a mask).
phenomena.record: per clothing noun: its verb (穿 / 戴)

model.other: no clothing field yet

phenomena.gap: The clothing field with a per-noun verb (穿 / 戴) and a choose exercise.

phenomena.title: Old and young: 老 / 旧, 年轻 / 新, 大 / 小
phenomena.alsoNote: Thai, Japanese and Korean also split 'old' for people and for things.
phenomena.what: ‘Old’ splits: 老 for people, animals and long-standing relations, 旧 for used things; ‘new’ is 新 for things, but ‘young’ for people is 年轻. Age comparison uses 大 / 小 with 比: 他比我大两岁 ‘he is two years older than me’.

examples.note: He is two years older than me.

phenomena.title: Rice: raw 米 vs cooked 饭
phenomena.what: Raw rice grains are 米 (on the plant 稻子), cooked rice is 米饭 or 饭, and 饭 also means ‘a meal’ (吃饭 ‘to eat, have a meal’).

phenomena.title: 借: borrow and lend in one verb
phenomena.alsoNote: Vietnamese mượn and Thai ยืม mean 'borrow' and become 'lend' with cho / ให้ 'give' before them.
phenomena.what: 借 means both ‘borrow’ and ‘lend’; the direction comes from the construction: 跟 / 向 someone 借 ‘borrow from’, 借给 someone ‘lend to’.

phenomena.title: ‘Play’ splits by activity
phenomena.what: There is no single ‘play’: 打 for ball games played with the hands and cards (打篮球, 打牌), 踢 for football (踢足球), 弹 for plucked or keyboard instruments (弹钢琴), 拉 for bowed ones (拉小提琴), 玩 for games and having fun (玩游戏).

phenomena.title: Time words: 时候 vs 时间, 点 vs 小时, 分 vs 分钟
phenomena.alsoNote: Cantonese and Korean separate clock points from durations in a similar way (三點 / 三個鐘; 세 시 / 세 시간).
phenomena.what: Chinese separates points from amounts of time: 什么时候 ‘when (at what point)’ vs 时间 ‘time (an amount)’; 三点 ‘three o'clock’ vs 三个小时 ‘three hours’; 十分 ‘ten past’ (on the clock) vs 十分钟 ‘ten minutes’.

examples.translit: bā diǎn shí fēn · shí fēnzhōng

phenomena.title: ‘Again’: 再 (future) vs 又 (past)
phenomena.what: ‘Again’ depends on whether the repetition is still to come (再: 明天再来 ‘come again tomorrow’, and 再见 ‘see you again’) or has already happened (又: 他又来了 ‘he came again’).

model.other: 再 only inside 再见

phenomena.gap: Lexemes 再 and 又 and a contrast exercise.

phenomena.title: ‘Want’: 要 vs 想
phenomena.alsoNote: German makes a similar firm / polite split with wollen and möchten.
phenomena.what: 要 + noun is ‘want, ask for’ and 要 + verb is a firm ‘want to, will’; 想 + verb is a softer ‘would like to’ (想 also means ‘think’ and ‘miss’). ‘I don't want to’ is 我不想; 不要 is a command ‘don't!’.

examples.note: I'd like to go to China.

model.other: two lexemes for verb.want; trap in fn.negation

phenomena.title: Happy: 高兴, 开心, 快乐 (wishes)
phenomena.what: 高兴 and 开心 describe being glad or having fun; wishes use 快乐: 生日快乐 ‘happy birthday’, 新年快乐 ‘happy New Year’ (never *生日高兴).

model.other: 高兴 and 开心 are lexemes for adj.happy; 快乐 appears in 快 sense s4 and in a trap

phenomena.title: One syllable, many meanings
phenomena.alsoNote: Vietnamese words of Chinese origin behave in a similar way.
phenomena.what: Short, old words have many meanings, and compounds pick one: 天 ‘day’, ‘sky’, ‘weather’ (今天, 天空, 天气); 家 ‘home’, ‘family’, the measure word for businesses and the suffix ‘-ist’; 开 ‘open’, ‘drive’, ‘switch on’, ‘bloom’.

phenomena.title: ‘Cut’ by instrument
phenomena.what: There is no all-purpose ‘cut’: the verb names the instrument or the movement — 切 slicing with a knife (切菜 ‘cut vegetables’), 剪 with scissors (剪头发 ‘cut hair’), 砍 chopping with an axe or heavy blade (砍树 ‘fell a tree’), 割 cutting along with a sickle or blade (割草 ‘mow grass’), 锯 sawing.

examples.translit: qiē cài · jiǎn tóufa · kǎn shù

phenomena.title: ‘Carry’ by manner
phenomena.what: There is no general ‘carry’: the verb says how — 拿 in the hand, 提 hanging from the hand (a bag, a bucket), 抱 in both arms (a child), 背 on the back, 扛 on the shoulder, 端 held level in front (a bowl), 抬 lifted by two or more people, 带 have with one, take along.

examples.text: 抱孩子 · 背包 · 端菜
examples.translit: bào háizi · bēi bāo · duān cài
examples.note: carry a child in the arms · carry a bag on the back · carry a dish (held level)

phenomena.gap: Concepts and lexemes are not in the course; a field with pictures and a choose exercise (how is it carried?).

phenomena.title: 在: one verb for ‘be located’
phenomena.what: ‘Be somewhere’ is one general verb 在 for people and things alike (书在桌子上 ‘the book is on the table’, 他在家 ‘he is at home’); no posture has to be chosen. When the posture matters, a posture verb + 着 is used, often with the place first (墙上挂着一张画 ‘a picture hangs on the wall’, 门口站着一个人 ‘someone is standing at the door’).

examples.note: The book is on the table. — no ‘lie / stand’ needed

examples.translit: Qiáng shang guàzhe yì zhāng huà.
examples.note: A picture hangs on the wall.

phenomena.gap: 着 is taught in cr.02 (坐着, 开着); posture verbs other than 坐 (站, 躺) are not in the course.

phenomena.title: Loanwords: sound, meaning, or both
phenomena.what: Foreign words are taken in three ways: by sound with characters chosen for their reading (咖啡 kāfēi, 沙发 shāfā), by translating the meaning (电脑 ‘electric brain’ = computer, 手机), or by both at once (啤酒 pí ‘beer’ + 酒 ‘alcoholic drink’; 冰淇淋 ‘ice’ + qílín). Meaning translations are preferred, so many internationally shared words appear as native-looking compounds.

examples.text: 咖啡 · 沙发 · 沙拉

phenomena.title: Mainland and Taiwan words
phenomena.what: The standard varieties of the mainland (普通话) and Taiwan (國語) differ in a number of everyday words, and the same word can mean different things: 土豆 is ‘potato’ in Beijing but ‘peanut’ in Taiwan. North and south also differ (西红柿 / 番茄 ‘tomato’).

phenomena.title: Written and spoken pairs
phenomena.what: Many concepts have a neutral or spoken word and a formal or written one, often a single classical morpheme or a 之- word: 妈妈 / 母亲, 爸爸 / 父亲, 老公 / 丈夫, 以后 / 之后, 以前 / 之前, 没有 / 无. The register must match the text.

phenomena.title: Four-character idioms (成语)
phenomena.alsoNote: Vietnamese also uses Sino-Vietnamese four-syllable idioms (thành ngữ).
phenomena.what: Chengyu are fixed four-character expressions, mostly from classical texts, often with a story behind them. They are frequent in writing and educated speech and cannot be understood word by word.

phenomena.title: Two-part allegorical sayings (歇后语)
phenomena.what: A xiehouyu is a riddle-like saying in two parts; the speaker often says only the first part and the listener supplies the second, which frequently rests on a pun.

examples.note: a nephew carrying a lantern — lights his uncle (照舅), i.e. ‘as before’ (照旧)

phenomena.title: Few light-verb combinations
phenomena.what: Most actions have their own verb or verb-object word (游泳 ‘swim’, 跳舞 ‘dance’). Only a handful of general verbs combine with nouns: 打 (打电话 ‘make a phone call’, 打球 ‘play ball’), 做 (做饭 ‘cook’, 做作业 ‘do homework’), and in formal writing 进行 / 加以 + a verbal noun (进行讨论 ‘hold a discussion’).

examples.text: 做饭 · 打电话 · 进行讨论
examples.translit: zuò fàn · dǎ diànhuà · jìnxíng tǎolùn
examples.note: cook · make a phone call · hold a discussion (formal)

phenomena.title: Lucky and unlucky homophones
phenomena.alsoNote: Japanese and Korean avoid 4 for the same reason (shi / sa sound like 'death').
phenomena.what: Sound-alikes carry luck: 四 sì sounds like 死 sǐ ‘die’ (no 4th floor), 八 bā like 发 fā ‘get rich’, 鱼 yú like 余 yú ‘surplus’ (fish at New Year: 年年有余). A clock is never a gift (送钟 sòng zhōng sounds like 送终 ‘attend a deathbed’).

examples.note: may every year have a surplus (fish = surplus)

model.other: fun facts on 四 and others

phenomena.gap: A culture note in fd.05 (numbers) linking the facts, and quiz items.

phenomena.title: Names: surname first
phenomena.alsoNote: Japanese, Hungarian and Vietnamese also put the family name first; Japanese titles follow the name too (田中先生).
phenomena.what: The surname comes first and is usually one syllable (王, 李, 张), followed by a one- or two-syllable given name: 王小明. Titles follow the name (王老师). Asking politely for someone's surname is 您贵姓？

examples.note: — What is your (honourable) surname? — My surname is Wang.

model.other: 贵 sense s3 (honorific); names are tokens with name: true in the bank

phenomena.gap: A greetings block on names and 姓 / 叫, and 姓 as a lexeme.

phenomena.title: Greeting by asking: 吃了吗？, 去哪儿？
phenomena.what: Among acquaintances, a common greeting is a question about what the other is doing — 吃了吗？ ‘have you eaten?’, 去哪儿啊？ ‘where are you off to?’ — not a real inquiry; a short answer is enough. 你好 is more for strangers; 你好吗 is a real question about someone you have not seen for a while.

examples.translit: — Chī le ma? — Chī le, nǐ ne?
examples.note: — Have you eaten? — Yes, and you?

model.other: fn.greetings summary and the funFact of 吃

phenomena.title: Modesty and declining compliments
phenomena.what: A compliment is traditionally deflected rather than accepted with ‘thank you’: 哪里哪里 ‘not at all’ (literally ‘where, where?’), 过奖了 ‘you flatter me’. Younger speakers say 谢谢 more often.

examples.translit: — Nǐ de Zhōngwén hěn hǎo! — Nǎli nǎli.
examples.note: — Your Chinese is very good! — Oh, not at all.

model.other: 哪里 sense s3

phenomena.gap: A pragmatics block and dialogue_turn items.

phenomena.title: Degrees of apology and attention
phenomena.what: 对不起 is a real apology; 不好意思 is a lighter ‘sorry, excuse me’ for small things and embarrassment; 打扰一下 and 劳驾 get attention or ask a favour. ‘That's all right’ after an apology is 没关系, after thanks 不客气.

examples.translit: Bù hǎoyìsi, wǒ lái wǎn le.

model.other: lexemes 对不起, 不好意思, 打扰一下, 劳驾

phenomena.title: No grammatical mirative
phenomena.what: Surprise or newly discovered information has no grammatical form; it is expressed with words — 原来 ‘so it turns out’, 竟然 / 居然 ‘unexpectedly, actually’ — and with the sentence-final particle 啊 and intonation.
phenomena.gap: Not said; 原来, 竟然 and 啊 are not in the course.

phenomena.title: No grammar of the speaker’s sex
phenomena.what: Grammar and vocabulary do not depend on the speaker’s sex: men and women use the same pronouns, verb forms and polite words. Some sentence-final particles and a coy, childlike style (撒娇 sājiāo) are heard more often from women, but this is style, not grammar.

examples.note: I am tired. — the same sentence for any speaker

model.other: fn.overview comparison notes (D18) for el, ru, hi, mr

phenomena.gap: Said in the overview notes for el, ru, hi and mr (D18: 我累了 for a man and a woman); not yet for the other learners whose languages mark the speaker’s sex (es, fr, ar, he, ja, ko).

phenomena.title: No speech levels or honorific verb forms
phenomena.what: There are no speech levels and no honorific forms of verbs: the grammar is the same towards a child and towards a minister. Respect is expressed by words — 您 ‘you (polite)’, titles (王老师), polite verbs and phrases (请 ‘please’, 贵姓 ‘your honourable surname’, 光临 ‘honour with a visit’) — and by modest words about oneself.

examples.note: Please sit down. · May I ask your surname? — politeness in the words, not in a verb form

model.other: fn.greetings teaches 您, 请 and 您贵姓; its comparison notes (D18) for ko and ja and the overview note for ko say that Chinese has no speech levels

phenomena.title: No optative: wishes with 祝
phenomena.what: There is no optative mood. Wishes are said with the verb 祝 ‘wish’ (祝你生日快乐 ‘happy birthday’, 祝你好运 ‘good luck’), with 希望 ‘hope’ or 但愿 ‘if only’, or as fixed formulas (新年快乐 ‘happy New Year’).
phenomena.gap: 祝 and 快乐 are not in the course; a wish formula block (with zh.sem.wishes).

phenomena.title: Fully regular number words
phenomena.what: Numbers are built like sums and products of 一 to 十, 百, 千: 十一 ‘ten-one’ = 11, 二十 ‘two-ten’ = 20, 九十九 = 99. There are no teens or tens words to learn, and no gender or case.

model.other: lexemes num.0–num.1000

phenomena.title: 两 and 二 for ‘two’
phenomena.what: Before a measure word ‘two’ is 两 (两个人, 两点 ‘two o'clock’); when counting, inside larger numbers and in ordinals it is 二 (十二, 二十, 第二). 两 can also mean ‘a couple of’.

model.other: two lexemes for num.2 with traps

phenomena.title: Counting in ten-thousands: 万 and 亿
phenomena.what: Large numbers are grouped by four digits: 万 = 10,000 and 亿 = 100,000,000 are the units. ‘A hundred thousand’ is 十万 (ten ten-thousands), ‘a million’ 一百万 (a hundred ten-thousands). Digits may still be written in groups of three, so reading a long number means regrouping it by four.

examples.text: 一万 · 十万 · 一百万

model.other: numbers stop at 一千

phenomena.gap: 万 and 亿 in the numbers of the core spine, and the number_words exercise.

phenomena.title: 零 for gaps inside numbers
phenomena.alsoNote: Vietnamese also says a word for the gap (một trăm lẻ / linh một '101'), but names each empty place in longer numbers.
phenomena.what: A missing place inside a number is said with 零 (once for any number of zeros): 一百零一 = 101, 一千零五 = 1005. 10 is 十, but 110 is 一百一十.

model.other: 零 sense s2; trap 十 vs 一十

phenomena.title: Ordinals with 第 — and numbers without it
phenomena.what: Ordinals put 第 before the number (第一 ‘first’, 第二天 ‘the second day’). Floors, dates, days of the week and months use the bare number: 三楼 ‘third floor’, 五号 ‘the 5th’, 星期一 ‘Monday’, 一月 ‘January’.

examples.translit: sān lóu · wǔ yuè wǔ hào

model.other: 第一 … 第十 (NUM, num.ord.1–10) and 第 (role, for every other number and 第几); fn.ordinals lists the bare-number ordinals (months, dates, floors, centuries, decades)

phenomena.title: Approximate numbers: 几, 多, 三四个
phenomena.what: Approximation is built in: two neighbouring numbers together (三四个人 ‘three or four people’), 多 after a round number (一千多 ‘over a thousand’), 几 for ‘a few’ (十几个 ‘a dozen or so’, 几个朋友 ‘a few friends’).

model.other: senses 多 s2, 几 s2

phenomena.gap: Bank sentences and a short block in a numbers step.

phenomena.title: Fractions and percent: the whole first
phenomena.what: Fractions and percentages name the whole first: 三分之一 ‘one third’ (of three parts, one), 百分之五十 ‘50 %’ (of a hundred parts, fifty). 半 ‘half’ is special: 三点半 ‘half past three’, 半个小时 ‘half an hour’.

model.other: 半 is a lexeme (S15)

phenomena.gap: Fractions and percent in the numbers of the core spine.

phenomena.title: Dates and times from big to small
phenomena.what: Dates and times go from the largest unit to the smallest: year – month – day – weekday – part of day – hour – minute. 2026年10月8日 星期四 上午九点 is ‘Thursday 8 October 2026, 9 a.m.’.

examples.translit: èr líng èr liù nián shí yuè bā rì, xīngqīsì

model.other: trap *一号五月

phenomena.title: Numbered weekdays and months
phenomena.what: Weekdays are ‘week-one’ to ‘week-six’ from Monday (星期一 … 星期六), and Sunday is 星期天 / 星期日 (‘week-day (sun)’); months are ‘one-month’ to ‘twelve-month’ (一月 … 十二月). 周一 and 礼拜一 are common alternatives to 星期一.
phenomena.record: variants: 周一 / 礼拜一 for each 星期 day

model.other: 星期一 … 星期日 lexemes; trap about Greek Δευτέρα

phenomena.gap: The alternatives 周一 … 周日 and 礼拜一 … 礼拜天 (very common in writing and speech) are not recorded as variants.

phenomena.title: The lunar calendar, festivals and the zodiac
phenomena.alsoNote: Japanese keeps the twelve animals but celebrates New Year on 1 January; Mongolian and Tibetan have their own lunisolar New Year with the twelve animals.
phenomena.what: Alongside the Gregorian calendar, the traditional lunisolar calendar (农历) fixes the festivals — 春节 Spring Festival, 中秋节 Mid-Autumn — and each year has one of twelve animals (生肖): 2026 is a Year of the Horse. Birthdays may be counted in either calendar.

examples.note: I was born in the Year of the Horse.

model.other: 年 sense ‘the New Year’, 丑 ‘second Earthly Branch’

phenomena.gap: A culture block in fd.15 (months and the year) and lexemes 春节, 农历.

phenomena.title: Asking and counting age
phenomena.alsoNote: Traditional Korean age also counted a newborn as one.
phenomena.what: Age is a number + 岁 without 是 (我二十岁). The question depends on whom you ask: 你几岁？ to a child, 你多大？ to a peer, 您多大年纪？ to an older person. Traditionally a newborn counted as one year old (虚岁).

examples.note: How old are you? (to an elderly person)

model.other: 岁 CLF lexeme; trap 你几岁 to an adult

phenomena.title: Money: 块 / 毛 spoken, 元 / 角 written
phenomena.alsoNote: Cantonese has the same written / spoken split with its own spoken words (蚊, 毫).
phenomena.what: The yuan is 元 in writing but 块 in speech; a tenth is 角 (written) or 毛 (spoken), a hundredth 分. Prices are said with 钱: 五块钱 ‘five yuan’, 三块五 ‘3.50’.

model.other: 块 role mentions ‘yuan’; 钱, 元, 毛 are not lexemes

phenomena.gap: A money step (with shopping: 多少钱, 块, 毛, 钱) and number exercises with prices.

phenomena.title: Colours: adjective and noun forms, and their meanings
phenomena.alsoNote: Japanese 青, Korean 푸르다 and Vietnamese xanh also cover both green and blue.
phenomena.what: Basic colours have a short adjective (红 ‘red’) and a noun with 色 ‘colour’ (红色 ‘red (colour)’). Green 绿 lǜ and blue 蓝 lán are two basic colours; the older 青 covers green, blue and black shades in set words (青菜 ‘green vegetables’, 青天 ‘blue sky’). Colours carry cultural meaning: red for luck and celebration, white for mourning, 黄色 also ‘pornographic’, and a ‘green hat’ (戴绿帽子) for a man whose partner cheats.

model.other: fd.17 has both forms as lexemes and the cultural senses

phenomena.title: Mandarin among the Chinese languages
phenomena.what: Mandarin (普通话 / 國語) is the standard, and its spoken and written forms are the same language, with no separate high variety. Cantonese, Wu, Min and Hakka, however, are separate Sinitic languages, mutually unintelligible with Mandarin though written with the same characters. Many Chinese speak a regional language at home, and dialect words appear in the standard (regional senses in the lexicon).

examples.text: 普通话 · 国语 · 华语

model.other: fn.overview facts

ADJ.title: pinyin (dictionary tones)
ADJ.why: The reading cannot be seen in the characters and the tones are part of the word. Dictionary (citation) tones, syllables separated by spaces; toneless syllables carry no mark; the spoken tones of 一 and 不 are in toneSandhi.

ADJ.title: traditional characters
ADJ.why: Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau write traditional characters; the learner meets both. The traditional form of the main meaning; other meanings in tradPerSense.

ADJ.title: reading per meaning (多音字)
ADJ.why: 长 cháng ‘long’ / zhǎng ‘to grow’, 都 dōu ‘all’ / dū ‘capital’: the reading depends on the meaning. Every reading with the senses it serves; none when all senses are read alike.

ADJ.title: traditional characters per meaning
